text.p: Silicon Graphics Inc executive vice-president Gary Lauer said on Thursday the company would continue gearing up production to tackle its highest order rate and backlog ever.
The graphics workstation-to-supercomputer maker said its consolidated backlog was worth $757 million at December 31, 1996, and product bookings hit $955 million -- both records for Silicon Graphics.
"We're very pleased with the acceptance of the new products," he said of the broadest product launch in the company's history last October. "We believe the momentum's actually building for them."
Analysts said management would also have to prove their ability to execute its production plan, which has been hampered by delays as they work to increase manufacturing output and meet demand.
"They have a problem. The problem is logistics," one analyst said. "They haven't been able to execute."
Lauer said the company would continue to build up production volumes, but declined to give specific figures.

"They're very complex technologies, so we're working through the production ramp and we think that the production ramp in our third quarter will be better than the second and the fourth better than our third," he said.
But Lauer would not say when the company would reach full production levels on the new products, adding Silicon Graphics may also accept running with higher inventory levels.

"One of the philosophical changes that we're making in our business is to run it with bigger backlogs, it gives us more breathing room to operate in," he said. "We're pleased that we are producing all the products. They're in manufacturing, they're working well and the order rates are very, very high."

Lauer spoke after the company reported a second fiscal quarter net loss of $12.9 million, or $0.07 a share, including a charge of $13.8 million, compared with net income of $52 million, or $0.30 a share, in the year-ago period. Revenues grew to $825 million, up from $672 million in the fiscal 1996 second quarter. Without the charge related to its acquisition of Cray Research last summer, the company would have reported net earnings per share of $0.01.
The stock ended down 7/8 at 27-1/4 in New York trading and the earnings report came after the market close.

Lauer repeated executives' earlier statement that they had sold around 10,000 of the new O2 workstations in the second quarter, adding it would sell "far in exess of that in the third quarter and the fourth quarter as well."
The executive declined to elaborate, but said the company would update its line of mid-range workstations on Monday.

The product transition comes at a difficult time in Silicon Graphics' market, as higher-end personal computers, powered by increasingly speedy Pentium Pro microprocessors made by Intel Corp, begin to eat into its market.

"The very broad issue for Silicon Graphics is one of competitiveness at the lower end of their product line," said Robert Herwick, who heads Herwick Capital Management. "At the high end the rest of the world's basically given up."
But Lauer pointed to favourable reviews of the company's O2 products in media publications and said the product had actually enabled it to reach deeper into the low-end market.

"What O2 has done is allowed us, because of the price and performance, to move down into market space where we didn't compete previously," he said. "We're doing it with performance, we're doing it with differentiation."
